encryption.could_not_create_key: Could not create the encryption key
encryption.disable_hint: Disabling is only possible while the share is empty. The server cannot decrypt anything already stored, so removing the key over existing content would make it permanently unreadable instead of restoring plain access.
encryption.enable_hint: Every file in this share is encrypted before it leaves your browser, using a key derived from the passphrase you type here. The passphrase itself never leaves the browser, and the server only ever stores ciphertext. Once this is on, the share becomes readable anywhere with rclone mount, using a crypt remote configured with this passphrase and the salt this screen will show you.
encryption.encrypted_note: End-to-end encrypted. Previews, the zip preview, and folder downloads are performed by this browser rather than the server, so they need the passphrase unlocked and are slower than on a plain share. They stream over a trusted TLS certificate; over this deployment's self-signed one, the browser refuses the background worker streaming needs, so a preview or download instead holds the whole file in memory, and a very large one is refused rather than attempted. SMB access and the Nextcloud and ownCloud sync clients still cannot read this share at all. It can still be read anywhere with rclone mount, using a crypt remote configured with this passphrase and the salt below.
encryption.passphrase_warning: Write this passphrase down and keep it safe. If it is lost, every file in this share becomes permanently unreadable: the server holds no key of its own and cannot recover it for you. The salt this creates is not secret and will stay visible on this share's row for as long as it is encrypted, but losing it is just as unrecoverable as losing the passphrase: rclone needs both together to read your files.
encryption.salt_copied: Salt for {name} copied to the clipboard.
encryption.share_not_empty: The share must be empty to change its encryption setting.
encryption.unlock_hint: This share is end-to-end encrypted. Enter its passphrase to continue.
encryption.verifier_note: This also stores a small probe encrypted under your key, so a mistyped passphrase next time is caught immediately instead of silently writing under the wrong key. It means anyone who steals the database could attempt an offline dictionary attack against your passphrase, starting from the moment encryption is on, even before the share holds any files.

upload_settings.cache_spool_enable: Spool chunks to the cache volume
upload_settings.cache_spool_hint: Off by default: chunks are written straight into the destination folder. Turn this on when the network is faster than the destination disk. Chunks then land in the cache directory under the data directory (mount a tmpfs or an NVMe volume there for a faster or larger one) and are merged into the destination continuously, so the cache never holds more than a fifth of that volume’s free space. An upload already in flight keeps the mode it started with.
upload_settings.cache_spool_unavailable: This deployment has no cache spool, so the switch has no effect.
upload_settings.concurrency_limit_hint: Maximum number of chunks and sessions sent concurrently. Can be set between 1 and 16 (default 4). Higher values increase throughput on fast networks, while lower values improve stability on unreliable connections.

upload_settings.saved_uploads_started_fr: Saved. Uploads started from now on send in {size} pieces.
upload_settings.two_values_below_apply_s: The two values below apply server-wide, to every account, immediately: no restart needed, and they survive one. The chunk size of an upload already in flight is fixed when its session is created and does not change.
upload_settings.unlike_server_wide_setti: Unlike the server-wide setting above, this only decides the chunk size that uploads started next in this browser begin with; it affects no other account or browser. It cannot go below the server minimum. If a proxy rejects a chunk with 413 (too large) mid-upload, this value is automatically lowered and saved.

webdav.generic_hint: Cyberduck, WinSCP, and similar tools connect to the address above. This server requires HTTPS and HTTP Basic authentication with an app password.
webdav.linux_step_enter_url: Use the address below: these file managers take the WebDAV scheme rather than the plain one.
webdav.linux_step_open: Open the file manager and choose Connect to Server (GNOME Files), or press Ctrl+L and type the address (Dolphin).
webdav.macos_step_credentials: When asked for a name and password, use your account name and an app password.
webdav.macos_step_enter_url: Enter the server address shown above and click Connect.
webdav.macos_step_open_connect: In Finder, choose Go, then Connect to Server.
webdav.nfc_note: Filenames are stored normalized to Unicode NFC, so a name typed on macOS and the same name typed on Windows refer to the same file.
webdav.rclone_crypt_hint: A share with encryption turned on stores rclone's own crypt format, so add a second remote wrapping the first. The passphrase is the one set when encryption was turned on, and password2 is that share's salt, shown on its encryption settings. Names are not encrypted, which is why filename_encryption is off and suffix is none; leaving those at their defaults makes rclone look for files that are not there.
webdav.rclone_crypt_warning: Neither value can be recovered by this server: it holds no passphrase and no key. Lose the passphrase and the files stay encrypted for good.
webdav.rclone_hint: rclone mounts this server on Linux, macOS and Windows, and is the only client listed here that can read an encrypted share. Put this in your rclone configuration, replacing SHARE with a folder name from the file list and ACCOUNT with your account name. Run rclone obscure to produce the password value.
